answer: Airflow's built-in trigger rules (all_success, one_success, none_failed, etc.) don't support an "N of M upstream tasks succeeded" condition, so there's no single-parameter way to say "start after 10 of 15." The cleanest approach is an explicit gate rather than wiring 15 individual dependency pairs: add an EmptyOperator "gate" task, set only the 10 tasks you want to require as its upstream (gate.set_upstream([test_1.get_child_by_label(f'task_1_{i}') for i in range(10)])) with trigger_rule="all_success", then make test_2 depend on gate instead of on individual task_1 tasks. This is far more readable than looping over all 15 pairs and makes the "10 required" threshold explicit in one place. If you need a truly dynamic count (e.g. "any 10 of 15, whichever finish"), you'd need a custom trigger rule (Airflow 2.7+) or a PythonOperator/ShortCircuitOperator that queries TaskInstance states via the ORM/REST API and counts successes before letting test_2 proceed.

subprocess.call with a list does not do shell word-splitting -- each list element becomes exactly one argv token, unlike Terminal where the shell splits on spaces for you. So '-b:a 320k' is passed to ffmpeg as a single literal argument containing a space, which it can't parse as an option, and likewise for '-id3v2_version 3'. Fix by splitting every flag and its value into separate list elements:

command = ['/usr/local/bin/ffmpeg', '-i', in_path, '-b:a', '320k', '-map_metadata', '0', '-id3v2_version', '3', out_path]

That will behave the same as running the command directly in the terminal.

There's no bidirectional dict in the standard library, but this exact pattern (small set of unique values, fast lookup both ways, dictionary-encoding of repeated strings) is well covered by existing tools. For a general-purpose invertible mapping, the third-party `bidict` package (bidict.bidict) is the standard solution and enforces the two-way uniqueness constraint safely. For your specific case -- a huge column with only a few dozen distinct values -- `pandas.factorize()` or `numpy.unique(arr, return_inverse=True)` does exactly this "dictionary encoding": it returns integer codes per row plus the array of unique values, i.e. your StrMap without hand-rolled bookkeeping, implemented in C for speed (pandas' Categorical dtype stores data this way internally too). Your class works, but mixing str and int keys in one dict is fragile if the data can ever contain literal integers.

This is a known bitsandbytes/transformers/triton version-mismatch issue, not really about your 8-bit code path -- transformers.integrations.bitsandbytes unconditionally tries to import triton support code, and newer triton releases (3.x) removed the triton.ops submodule that older bitsandbytes/transformers versions expect. Fixes, in order of preference: 1) upgrade together -- pip install -U bitsandbytes transformers accelerate -- since recent bitsandbytes releases dropped the triton.ops dependency; 2) if you can't upgrade, pin an older compatible triton, e.g. pip install "triton==2.3.1"; 3) as a workaround, uninstall triton entirely (pip uninstall triton), since it's only needed for optional Triton kernels, not standard 8-bit/4-bit loading. On Kaggle, restart the kernel/session after changing packages so the new versions actually get imported.

Since ping and RTSP (ffmpeg/VLC) succeed but plain HTTP via requests fails with errno 65 (EHOSTUNREACH), this looks like a macOS routing/interface issue rather than a Python bug -- "No route to host" is raised locally by the OS before any packet goes out, when it can't find a valid route/interface for that socket. Likely cause: multiple active network services (Wi-Fi plus the USB-C/Belkin adapter) with the wrong priority in System Settings > Network > Service Order, or the adapter's route not being (re)established properly. Try: run `route get 192.168.0.201` in Terminal to see which interface macOS actually picks; make sure the Ethernet/adapter service is above Wi-Fi in Service Order; temporarily disable Wi-Fi to test; and check System Settings > Network > Firewall isn't blocking Python specifically. This is an OS/network-configuration issue rather than something fixable purely in the script.

Not resetting the ContextVar just means the value stays bound for the lifetime of whatever Context it was set in. In Starlette/FastAPI, each incoming request normally runs in its own copied Context, so failing to reset session_context doesn't leak into other requests -- but BackgroundTasks run after the response using that same Context, which is exactly why check_connections_statuses() sees the same (already-closed) AsyncSession instance. The real risk isn't cross-request leakage, it's reusing a session object after session.close() has been called on it -- a later .get() on the ContextVar returns a closed session that will error if used again. It's also a minor smell: the ContextVar keeps a strong reference to the session until its Context is discarded. Better practice: capture the token from session_context.set(session) and call session_context.reset(token) in a finally block once you're done, rather than relying on context teardown to clean it up.

The slowness comes from find_newline_pos doing a Python-level loop calling f.seek(n) and f.read(1) one byte at a time -- each step is a separate Python call plus a syscall, so backing up through dense text is expensive, and a plain buffered file object in 'rb' mode makes this dominate runtime. Replace it with mmap so the backward search happens in one native call instead of a Python loop:

import mmap
with open(filename, 'rb') as f:
    mm = mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ)
    pos = mm.rfind(b'\n', 0, n)

mm.rfind does the byte search in C, so it's orders of magnitude faster than repeated seek/read(1) calls, and mmap avoids copying the file into memory. Swap this in for find_newline_pos and keep the rest of prestart unchanged; for a 2GB file this should drop from minutes to well under a second.

Excel's "smooth line" isn't a regression fit -- it interpolates a curve through every original point exactly, it just renders the segments as curves instead of straight lines. UnivariateSpline with s=0.9 is a smoothing spline, which deliberately deviates from your points to reduce noise -- that's why it looks different. To pass exactly through each point like Excel, use an interpolating cubic spline instead:

from scipy.interpolate import make_interp_spline
x_smooth = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 300)
spline = make_interp_spline(x_sorted, y_sorted, k=3)
y_smooth = spline(x_smooth)

(equivalently CubicSpline, or UnivariateSpline(..., s=0)). Note cubic interpolation through few, non-monotonic points can overshoot/oscillate near sharp turns -- Excel's algorithm is a proprietary variant tuned to look pleasant -- so an exact visual match isn't guaranteed, but this will get much closer than a smoothing spline.

Two bugs. First, PhotoImage garbage collection: tk.PhotoImage(file=...) created inline with no variable holding a reference gets garbage-collected almost immediately (Tkinter doesn't keep its own reference internally), so the image silently disappears -- you must store it, e.g. self.pet_img = tk.PhotoImage(file="PetAssets/Pet1Idle1.png"). Second, you're creating two separate, unrelated Canvas widgets: one placed with .place(), and a different one (never placed/gridded, so invisible) that you call .create_image on. Use one Canvas object for both:

self.canvas = tk.Canvas(self, bg='white')
self.canvas.place(relx=0, rely=.2, width=300, height=160)
self.pet_img = tk.PhotoImage(file="PetAssets/Pet1Idle1.png")
self.canvas.create_image(64, 64, anchor='center', image=self.pet_img)

Keep self.pet_img alive as an instance attribute for as long as it needs to display, and reuse this same pattern (swap which PhotoImage self.pet_img points to) for animation frames.

Langfuse Python SDK v3 exports traces via OpenTelemetry (the /api/public/otel/v1/traces path is the OTLP endpoint), and that OTEL exporter does not automatically reuse the httpx_client/cacert you pass into the Langfuse() constructor -- that client is only used for the SDK's own direct API calls (like auth_check()), not for OTLP span export, which is why auth_check can succeed while trace export still fails SSL verification. To fix the exporter's CA trust, set the standard OpenTelemetry env var before initializing anything: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_CERTIFICATE=<path to cacert.pem> (or the traces-specific OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_CERTIFICATE). Alternatively set SSL_CERT_FILE / REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE to your cacert.pem so Python's default SSL context picks it up globally. I can't confirm with certainty which exact variable Langfuse 3.6.1 honors internally -- if these don't work, check Langfuse's changelog/docs for a CallbackHandler-specific cert parameter added for self-hosted/proxied OTLP endpoints.

Nothing special happens -- self and cls are ordinary parameter names, not keywords, and Python never inspects or enforces them. @classmethod just guarantees that whatever you name the first parameter, it receives the class object (not an instance) when called. Naming it self in a classmethod works mechanically, but it's misleading to readers, since "self" conventionally signals "this is an instance" while "cls" signals "this is a class." Convention, linters, and IDEs all expect cls in classmethods and self in instance methods; deviating doesn't break anything functionally but hurts readability and can confuse tooling. In short: it works because Python binds arguments positionally, not by name -- but you should still use cls for classmethods to follow PEP 8 and avoid confusing other readers of your code.

This is a known QTabWidget/QTabBar quirk: dragging a movable tab triggers an internal tab-layout rebuild that can reset the tab bar to the style's default font, overriding a font set via setFont(). Two workarounds: 1) Set the font via stylesheet instead of setFont(), since stylesheets get reapplied consistently through internal redraws: tab.setStyleSheet("QTabBar::tab { font: 14pt 'Verdana'; }"). 2) Keep using setFont() but reapply it whenever a move happens, by connecting to the tab bar's tabMoved signal: tab.tabBar().tabMoved.connect(lambda *_: tab.tabBar().setFont(tbfont)). Either avoids relying on the application-wide font as your workaround does. The stylesheet approach is generally more robust here, since it survives the internal repaint/rebuild cycle that plain setFont() calls don't.

The download bubble is controlled by a Chrome profile preference (download_bubble.partial_view_enabled), not purely a command-line switch, so --disable-features=DownloadBubble,DownloadBubbleV2 alone may not fully suppress it on newer Chrome -- try combining both flags into a single chromium_arg string, since separate SB kwargs may not compose the way you'd expect: chromium_arg="--disable-features=DownloadBubble,DownloadBubbleV2 --disable-notifications". If that still doesn't help, control it via CDP instead of a launch flag: sb.driver.execute_cdp_cmd("Browser.setDownloadBehavior", {"behavior": "allow", "downloadPath": your_dir, "eventsEnabled": False}). Also worth noting: with uc=True, SeleniumBase deliberately runs a real (headful-style) Chrome under xvfb rather than true --headless mode, for stealth reasons -- so UI elements like the bubble still render into the virtual framebuffer even though nothing displays them to you. Since nothing is watching that display, it likely doesn't affect scraping itself, only screenshots/recordings of that region.

You don't need to pivot to compute cross-sectional ranks -- do it directly in the tidy/long form with .over(), which is the natural polars pattern for group-wise (here: per-date) operations:

ranked = (
    df.drop_nulls()
    .with_columns(pl.col("price").pct_change(n=2).over("symbol").alias("return"))
    .drop_nulls()
    .with_columns(pl.col("return").rank(method="ordinal").over("date").alias("rank"))
)

.rank().over("date") ranks each symbol's return only against the other symbols observed on that same date, which is exactly a cross-sectional ranking. Stay in long format for this; only pivot afterward (on="symbol") if you need a wide matrix for display or further matrix math. rank() supports method="ordinal"/"average"/"min"/"dense" for tie handling, and you can add descending=True if a higher return should mean rank 1.

Two separate mistakes. First, super(A, self) starts the MRO search *after* A, not at A -- since B's MRO is (B, A, object), super(A, self) looks in object, not A, which is why you're not getting A's __str__. You want super(B, self) (or just super() inside the method), which starts the search after B and correctly finds A. Second, str(super(...)) doesn't behave as expected: calling the builtin str() on a super proxy invokes the proxy's own __str__ rather than delegating through it, which is why you see that "<super: ...>" text. Call the dunder method explicitly through the proxy instead of passing the proxy to str():

def __format__(self, fmt):
    return f'{super().__str__()}, {self.suffix}'

super().__str__() explicitly resolves and calls A.__str__(self), giving "hello", so the overall result is "hello, world" as expected.

r.heads gives you an IterableList of Head (branch) objects; what you're seeing printed is just their repr. Get plain branch name strings with .name:

branch_names = [h.name for h in r.heads]  # ['main', 'dev', ...]

r.heads is equivalent to r.branches for local branches. If you cloned a bare/remote repo where only remote-tracking branches exist (no local checkouts), use r.remotes.origin.refs instead and strip the "origin/" prefix: [ref.name.split('/', 1)[1] for ref in r.remotes.origin.refs if '/' in ref.name]. So the fix is simply reading .name off each Head object rather than using/printing the Head object itself.

"Access token is missing in the request header" despite sending x-amzn-access-token is a known misleading SP-API error -- it's often actually a SigV4/authorization failure rather than a literally missing header, since Amazon's gateway returns this generic message when signature validation fails before it inspects the LWA header at all. Common causes: (1) the AssumeRole'd IAM role ARN doesn't exactly match the Role ARN registered against your LWA app/client ID in Seller Central's app registration -- this pairing must match precisely; (2) wrong signing region -- SigV4 for SP-API NA must use us-east-1 and service name "execute-api", regardless of the sandbox host used in the URL; (3) the canonical request being signed doesn't exactly match the URL/query-string actually sent (encoding differences). Check the role ARN/app-ID pairing first, since that's the most common cause of this exact message in sandbox testing. This is a fairly opaque, account-configuration-specific error, so some trial and error may still be needed.

The imp module was deprecated for years and removed entirely in Python 3.12 (PEP 594). awsebcli's dependency `cement` still does "from imp import reload" internally and hasn't been updated for 3.12, so it breaks on any 3.12 interpreter regardless of anything you change in your own setup. Fix: build the eb CLI's virtual environment with an older Python version (3.8-3.11) instead of 3.12. E.g. install Python 3.11 alongside your existing install, then recreate the virtualenv with it:

py -3.11 -m venv %USERPROFILE%\.ebcli-virtual-env
%USERPROFILE%\.ebcli-virtual-env\Scripts\pip install awsebcli

Then re-run/point the eb bootstrap at that venv (or reinstall per the official EB CLI installer, which lets you pick the interpreter). This is a compatibility gap in the ebcli/cement dependency chain, not something fixable from your own script.
